meta.title: Who really said "I don't want a nation of thinkers, I want a nation of workers"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No source has ever been cited for this Rockefeller line. Wikiquote calls it Disputed, Snopes rates it Unproven — it traces to a 2006 conspiracy documentary.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I don't want a nation of thinkers, I want a nation of workers'?
meta.ogDescription: Rockefeller is not recorded saying it. Wikiquote calls it Disputed and Snopes Unproven; Snopes suggests it is a loose paraphrase of a 1913 pamphlet by his adviser Frederick T. Gates.

answer.label: Not John D. Rockefeller — an undocumented paraphrase of Frederick T. Gates
answer.authorDates: 1853–1929 · Baptist minister; Rockefeller’s principal philanthropic adviser
answer.sourceLine: No speech, letter, interview, or book has ever been cited for this line, and Rockefeller is not recorded saying it — Wikiquote lists it under Disputed ↗ and Snopes rates it Unproven ↗. The nearest documented text is a passage that Rockefeller’s adviser Frederick T. Gates published in The Country School of To-morrow (1913) ↗, which Snopes calls the likely source of the paraphrase — but Gates did not write these words either, and what he actually wrote says something narrower.

source.heading: The nearest documented source

docMeta.dd: None — no speech, letter, interview, or book has ever been cited
Frederick T. Gates, whose title page names him chairman of the General Education Board
General Education Board, Occasional Papers, No. 1 (New York, 1913); reprinted 1916

source.excerpt: Is there aught of remedy for this neglect of rural life? Let us, at least, yield ourselves to the gratifications of a beautiful dream that there is. In our dream, we have limitless resources, and the people yield themselves with perfect docility to our molding hand. The present educational conventions fade from our minds; and, unhampered by tradition, we work our own good will upon a grateful and responsive rural folk. We shall not try to make these people or any of their children into philosophers or men of learning or of science. We are not to raise up from among them authors, orators, poets, or men of letters. We shall not search for embryo great artists, painters, musicians. Nor will we cherish even the humbler ambition to raise up from among them lawyers, doctors, preachers, politicians, statesmen, of whom we now have ample supply.
trail: Wikiquote places the line in its Disputed section ↗, noting that Jim Marrs attributed it in the William Lewis film One Nation Under Siege and that no published occurrence has been located before Marrs’s book The Trillion-Dollar Conspiracy (2010).

Snopes rates the claim Unproven ↗: there is no evidence Rockefeller or anyone else connected to the General Education Board said it, and the earliest reference Snopes could identify is the documentary, which it dates to 2006. (Wikiquote dates the film 2008; the two sources disagree, and the discrepancy is unresolved here.)

The wording that does exist in print is Gates’s. The Library of Congress record ↗ dates The Country School of To-morrow to 1913 and marks it public domain; Snopes cites it as 1916, which is a genuine later printing — also scanned ↗, with the same passage.
Quote Investigator ↗ has not published on this quote, so no earlier tracing exists to defer to; the claims above are the limit of what is documented.
source.cutTag: Not the quote — the nearest documented text
source.excerptNote: This is Gates, not Rockefeller, and it is not the quote — it is the passage Snopes identifies as the likely thing being paraphrased ↗. It appears on p. 6, under the heading “A Vision of the Remedy,” in the scanned 1913 pamphlet ↗. Two things get lost in the compression: Gates is describing a deliberate rhetorical “dream” about *rural* schooling, and a few lines later he hopes that if “a child of genius should spring up from the soil, that genius will surely bud and not be blighted.” Worth noting that Snopes’s own transcription of this passage is itself inexact — the wording above is taken from the scan.

source.rightsNote: Two separate questions. The popular one-liner has no identifiable author, work, or first publication, so there is no rights status to assert — it is not claimed as public domain here. The Gates passage shown above is a different matter: the Library of Congress dates it 1913 and states the collection is public domain ↗, well before the 1931 US threshold.

author.name: Frederick T. Gates
author.kicker: The nearest documented voice — not the author of this line
author.heading: Who actually wrote the passage behind the meme
author.metaLine: 1853–1929 · Baptist minister; Rockefeller's principal philanthropic adviser and chairman of the General Education Board
author.bio: A Baptist clergyman who pastored in Minneapolis before becoming John D. Rockefeller’s principal business and philanthropic adviser from 1891 to 1923, Gates is the figure who turned Rockefeller’s giving away from personal handouts and into large expert-run foundations. In 1913 he published The Country School of To-morrow for the General Education Board, a fifteen-page pamphlet whose deliberately dreamlike central passage — about not trying to make rural children into philosophers or poets — is almost certainly what the Rockefeller “quote” is a garbled memory of. He did not write the popular line, and no one has ever claimed he did; he is here because he is the only documented text anywhere near it.

cite.sourceCitation: Frederick T. Gates, The Country School of To-morrow, Publications of the General Education Board, Occasional Papers, No. 1 (New York: General Education Board, 1913), 6. The one-liner popularly attributed to John D. Rockefeller has no documented source; per Wikiquote, no published occurrence has been located earlier than Jim Marrs, The Trillion-Dollar Conspiracy (New York: William Morrow, 2010), and Snopes traces the earliest reference of any kind to the William Lewis documentary One Nation Under Siege.

copyAttribution: There is no evidence John D. Rockefeller ever said "I don't want a nation of thinkers, I want a nation of workers." Wikiquote lists it as Disputed; Snopes rates it Unproven. It entered circulation when Jim Marrs attributed it in the documentary One Nation Under Siege and printed it in The Trillion-Dollar Conspiracy (2010). The nearest documented text is Frederick T. Gates, The Country School of To-morrow (General Education Board, Occasional Papers No. 1, New York, 1913), p. 6 — which Gates framed as a "dream" about rural schooling, and which says something materially different.

misattribution.heading: How a line nobody can source became Rockefeller’s most quoted sentence
misattribution.intro: This is a quote with no document behind it. It is not a mangled transcription of something Rockefeller said in a hall on a known date — there is no hall and no date. Here is who gets named, and what each name is actually doing.

items.why: The credit everyone repeats, and the one with no evidence. Snopes found no evidence that Rockefeller or anyone else connected to the General Education Board said it ↗, and Wikiquote files it as Disputed rather than sourced ↗. Rockefeller founded and funded the General Education Board in 1903, which is why the line sticks to him so easily.

Marrs is not claimed as the author — he is the reason the sentence exists in public. Wikiquote credits him with the attribution in the William Lewis documentary One Nation Under Siege, and finds no published occurrence before his book The Trillion-Dollar Conspiracy (2010) ↗. Tellingly, the wording Snopes transcribes from the film is itself hedged ↗ — Marrs says Rockefeller “was quoted as saying” it, and prefaces the whole thing with “I think.” The certainty was added later, by everyone else.

Also not a rival claimant — nobody attributes the one-liner to him. Snopes proposes the line is a poor paraphrase of Gates ↗, and the 1913 pamphlet bears that out and undercuts it at once ↗: Gates writes about not raising up philosophers, poets, painters or lawyers from among *rural* families, explicitly inside “a beautiful dream,” and immediately adds that a child of genius must be able to bud “and not be blighted.” That is not the same claim as wanting a nation of workers.

Wikiquote’s note points to a similar phrase in an 1849 editorial by the Irish journalist William Cooke Taylor ↗. Flagged here for completeness only: that pointer could not be independently confirmed against the 1849 text, so no antecedent is asserted.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that no author has ever been documented for this sentence. It has a first known attributor ↗, a real 1913 passage it may be a faded memory of ↗, and a verdict of Unproven ↗ — but no source, and no Rockefeller.

context.heading: Why this one refuses to die
lead: Most unsourced quotes get repeated because they are pleasing. This one gets repeated because it is useful — it hands you a villain and a motive for everything you dislike about school in fourteen words. That is a much stronger engine than charm.

And it survives fact-checking because the surrounding history is not fake at all. Rockefeller really did create the General Education Board in 1903 and pour money into it, and Snopes quotes a 1992 history of the GEB describing how its programs repeatedly steered non-college students toward vocational offerings ↗. The quote is undocumented; the grievance it dramatises has real documents behind it.
detailsBody: There is a small irony buried in the paper trail. The man who put the line into circulation hedged it — “I think” Rockefeller “was quoted as saying” — and the fact-check that debunks it garbles the 1913 passage it holds up as the real thing. Each retelling sanded off a qualifier until an undocumented paraphrase was being quoted as a boast.

If you want the primary document rather than the meme, read Gates’s fifteen pages for yourself. It is stranger and more revealing than the slogan: a philanthropist openly fantasising about “limitless resources” and people who “yield themselves with perfect docility to our molding hand,” while insisting the goal is to make rural life “beautiful, intelligent, fruitful, recreative, healthful, and joyous.” The real text indicts a mindset far more precisely than the slogan does.
context.pull: The sentence is undocumented. The unease it speaks for is not — which is exactly why no amount of debunking retires it.
